excerpts.quote: The Black Death reached Iceland in 1402–1404 and again in 1494–1495, with devastating effects. The first outbreak is estimated to have killed 50–60% of the population, while the second resulted in a 30–50% mortality rate.

The population of the island is believed to have varied from 40,000 to 60,000 in the period ranging from initial settlement until the mid-19th century. ... The first census was carried out in 1703 and revealed that the population was then 50,358.
the plague did not reach Iceland until 1402

Sweden was reached also by the second and third European Black Death epidemic of 1359–1360 and 1368–1370. ... The plague also returned in repeated national epidemics in 1413, 1421–22, 1439–40, 1451, 1455, 1464–65, 1472–74 and 1495. ... After the Middle Ages, the plague returned in 1548–49, 1565–66, 1572, 1576, 1580, 1603, 1623, 1629–30, 1638, 1653 and 1657, before the Great Northern War plague outbreak in 1710–1713, which was to be the last outbreak of Bubonic plague in Sweden.

It has been suggested that the plague never reached Finland because the contacts between Sweden and Finland was disconnected during the Black Death or that it did reach Finland but had less impact, because the low population made it difficult for it to spread.
In 1361–1362 the plague returned to England, this time causing the death of around 20% of the population.

Over the following decades the plague would return—on a national or a regional level—at intervals of five to 12 years, with gradually dwindling death tolls. ... An outbreak in 1471 took as much as 10–15 per cent of the population, while the death rate of the plague of 1479–1480 could have been as high as 20 per cent. From that point outbreaks became fewer and more manageable, due largely to conscious efforts by central and local governments—from the late 15th century onward—to curtail the disease.

A study published in 2015 indicates that other Asiatic rodents served as plague reservoirs, from which infections spread as far west as Europe via trade routes, both overland and maritime. Although the black rat was certainly a plague vector in European ports, the spread of the plague beyond areas colonized by rats suggests that the plague was also circulated by humans after reaching Europe.
Although R. rattus populations often die out after a plague, causing transmission to cease, rats that survive the plague can serve as reservoirs for the disease

Between 1900 and 2015, the United States had 1,036 human plague cases, with an average of 9 cases per year. ... These US cases usually occur in rural northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon, and far western Nevada.
